author: N. B. Robinson
title: North Carolina Unified Champion Schools earn national honor from Special Olympics - West Wake News
text:
Eight schools in North Carolina have been selected for national banner recognition by Special Olympics North Carolina (SONC) for the 2024-25 school year. The recognition highlights their efforts to provide inclusive sports and activities for students with and without disabilities.
According to SONC President/CEO Keith L. Fishburne, “eight Special Olympics Unified Champion Schools in North Carolina are receiving national banner recognition for their efforts to provide inclusive sports and activities for students with and without disabilities for the 2024-25 school year.”
The recognized schools include Beverly Woods Elementary School, Bunn Middle School, Cramerton Middle School, Charles P. Murray Middle School, Duke University, Francis Bradley Middle School, Idlewild Elementary, and Swansboro High School. These schools will receive a banner to display on campus as part of the distinction.
The schools achieved this status by meeting ten national standards of excellence in inclusion, advocacy, and respect. These standards were created by a panel made up of leaders from both Special Olympics and the education sector.
Unified Champion Schools is a program that brings together students with and without intellectual disabilities through three main components: Unified Sports, inclusive youth leadership opportunities, and whole-school engagement. According to Special Olympics, about 19.5 million young people are participating in these types of inclusive experiences worldwide.
Currently, nearly 600 schools in North Carolina take part in Unified Champion Schools programming as part of more than 10,800 schools nationwide. The initiative has set a goal to reach 20,000 participating schools by 2030.
The model is supported by the Office of Special Education Programs at the U.S. Department of Education. Research has shown that it helps foster positive social relationships among students with and without disabilities while also promoting an inclusive climate within schools.
Special Olympics North Carolina was founded in 1968 and now serves nearly 53,000 athletes across the state. The organization provides training and competitions in twenty Olympic-type sports along with health initiatives aimed at improving access to community resources for individuals with intellectual disabilities.
